blocks.title: Track both the value and its type
paragraphs: A Java expression has a type as well as a value. Write down the operands’ types before calculating: they determine which operations Java performs, whether a conversion is needed and how a finite representation behaves.

blocks.title: Declaration is different from assignment
paragraphs: int count; declares a local variable. count = 6; gives it a value, and count = count + 2; reads the old value before storing 8. A local must be definitely assigned on every path before it is read. A field has a Java default value; that does not make an uninitialized local readable.

Use a type that represents the requirement: boolean for a condition, int for a bounded whole-number count and double for an approximate fractional measurement. The identifier denotes a variable, not a permanent mathematical equation.

blocks.title: A reference is a value that identifies an object
paragraphs: Primitive variables contain primitive values. A reference variable contains a reference to an object, or null; assigning one reference to another copies the reference, not the object. Mutating one shared object and reassigning one variable are different operations.

The declared type controls which operations the compiler permits. String is a reference type; char is a primitive UTF-16 code unit. The eight primitive types are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean. The valid short range is −32768 through 32767.

blocks.title: Evaluate using Java’s numeric and operator rules
paragraphs: Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition. In 3 + 2 * 4 the result is 11; parentheses change the grouping. With int operands, 11 / 4 is 2 and -11 / 4 is -2: integer division truncates toward zero. -11 % 4 is -3, so quotient * divisor + remainder reconstructs the dividend.

String concatenation is evaluated in expression order: "total=" + 2 + 3 produces "total=23", whereas "total=" + (2 + 3) produces "total=5". A displayed result is not evidence that the intended arithmetic happened.

blocks.title: Convert before the operation whose behavior must change
paragraphs: double average = count / groups; still divides two integers first. Use (double) count / groups when a fractional quotient is intended. Assigning that result later to a double cannot recover a discarded fraction.

A narrowing conversion may require an explicit cast and can lose information. Converting an ordinary finite value such as -3.9 to int gives -3, not -4. Widening from int to double preserves every int value, but not every widening numeric conversion preserves precision: large long values may lose low bits in double.

blocks.title: Finite numbers have boundaries
paragraphs: Java int arithmetic uses 32-bit signed values; overflow wraps without an overflow exception. Floating-point values approximate many decimal fractions: 0.1 + 0.2 need not equal the stored approximation of 0.3. Do not mistake approximate arithmetic for exact decimal calculation.

Distinguish failure kinds. An incompatible assignment can be rejected at compile time. Dividing an integer by a variable whose value is zero throws at runtime. A program that compiles and runs can still calculate the wrong result because it uses integer division where a fraction was intended.

blocks.title: Three conversions, three different effects
paragraphs: Trace each assignment before reading the output. The first line is 2.0 2.75 -126; the second is -2147483648. The cast affects either the operation’s input type or the stored result, depending on where it appears.

blocks.title: A four-question numeric check
paragraphs: Before trusting an expression, check the operand types, evaluation order, conversion position and representable range. Then classify a problem as compile-time rejection, runtime failure or a wrong result; each requires different evidence.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between int n; and n = 7;?
cards.answer: The first declares a local variable; the second assigns a value. A local cannot be read until Java can establish that it was assigned on that path.

cards.prompt: After int n = 4; n = n + 3;, what is n and why?
cards.answer: 7. Java evaluates the right-hand expression using the old value 4 and then assigns the resulting value to n.

cards.prompt: If two variables contain the same object reference, did assignment copy the object?
cards.answer: No. The variables contain copied references to the same object. Mutating that object can be observed through either reference; reassigning one variable changes only that variable.

cards.prompt: How do char, String and null differ?
cards.answer: char is a primitive UTF-16 code unit. String is a reference type. null is a value that can be assigned to reference variables, not to primitive variables.

cards.prompt: What are -11 / 4 and -11 % 4 for int operands?
cards.answer: -2 and -3. Division truncates toward zero, and (-2)*4 + (-3) equals -11.
The first performs left-to-right concatenation and produces x=23. Parentheses force numeric addition first in the second, producing x=5.
The first performs integer division before the cast and gives 2.0. The second converts an operand before division and gives 2.75.

cards.prompt: Does casting -3.9 to int round to the nearest integer?
cards.answer: No. For this finite in-range value, conversion truncates toward zero and produces -3. A cast is not a general rounding operation.

cards.prompt: What happens when an int variable holding Integer.MAX_VALUE is increased by one?
cards.answer: It wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, -2147483648. Java does not throw an integer-overflow exception for this addition.

cards.prompt: Why should a fractional measurement comparison allow an appropriate tolerance?
cards.answer: Many decimal values have only approximate binary floating-point representations. Select a tolerance justified by the problem rather than assuming every decimal calculation is exact.

guided.title: Audit a grouped measurement
guided.prompt: A program stores 11 samples in int count and 4 groups in int groups, then sets double average = count / groups. Explain the result, correct the fractional calculation, and classify these separate defects: reading an unassigned local, dividing by a zero-valued integer variable, and adding one to Integer.MAX_VALUE.

fields.label: Values and types before and after the calculation
Corrected expression and reason for conversion position

rubric: Identifies the original value as 2.0 and the intended fractional value as 2.75.
Places a double conversion on an operand before division.
Separates compile-time definite-assignment rejection from a runtime ArithmeticException.
Explains int wrapping rather than inventing an overflow exception; primitive values are not object references.
reference: count / groups evaluates as int 2 before assignment widens it to double 2.0. (double) count / groups gives 2.75.
An unassigned local read is a compile-time error. Integer division by a zero-valued variable throws ArithmeticException. Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 evaluates to -2147483648.
Other expressions that ensure floating-point division are valid. A correct audit explains the types and operations, not just the printed numbers.
